title: Was knife in Jermaine Carby's hand? Witnesses can't agree as police shooting inquest begins
article: Jermaine Carby's mother says she wants "the truth to come out and justice to be served" as an inquest into his 2014 shooting death by Peel Regional Police began in Brampton today.
Despite the Special Investigations Unit clearing the officers involved of any criminal wrongdoing, Lorna Robinson still blames them for the 33-year-old's death.

"I want them to recognize themselves that they did something wrong and that they say something to us," Robinson told reporters outside the Provincial Offences Court on Ray Lawson Boulevard. "I want them to own up to the fact that they did something wrong."

But the coroner's jury - four women and one man - will not assign blame to anyone in the three-week proceeding, presiding coroner Dr. William Lucas explained at the beginning of the inquest. It is their job to determine how Carby died, and come up with recommendations on any changes that can be made to prevent future similar deaths.
Fifteen witnesses are expected to testify.
Robinson told reporters that the fact the five inquest jurors are all white doesn't make a difference to her.
"It doesn't really matter whether they're black or white," she said. "I believe the Lord will work it out."
She said she wants to see the Peel Regional Police officer who shot and killed her son during the Sept. 24, 2014 traffic stop on Queen Street East just east of Kennedy Road around 10 p.m.

And she wants hear recommendations about the knife that was removed from Carby after he was shot, put in a paper bag and placed in a Peel police officer's cruiser until the SIU investigators arrived on scene.
"They should know better than to tamper with evidence," Robinson told reporters. "There must have been a reason it was moved. It wasn't there in the first place."

Jurors heard the knife was offered to an SIU investigator who arrived on scene, but he told the Peel officer to keep it until the forensic SIU investigator arrived. Coroner's counsel Michael Blain told jurors they will hear the forensic officer didn't immediately take the weapon from police, but conducted other scene duties before he took custody of it around 5 a.m. the next morning.
That information had not previously been released. The SIU slammed Peel police for holding onto the knife for hours before handing it over.
Jurors heard from two witnesses this morning. The first, Vanessa Mulcare, testified she saw the knife in Carby's hand as he walked slowly toward two or three officers, their guns drawn.

She told the SIU at the time that she didn't see the knife, but heard the officers yelling at Carby to "Drop the knife" as many as 10 times before he was shot. She was adamant Monday that she had seen the knife in Carby's hand.
"I don't feel that I'm making it up," she told jurors. "I can picture it."
She said she didn't think Carby should have been shot dead, but instead should have been shot in the arm or leg.

"I don't disagree with the amount of shots," she told the inquest. "My opinion was, did it have to be to the point where he was killed? Is there some other way he might have been shot to be stopped. To his arms or his legs..."
Richard Appleby, testified he was on a smoke break while working at a nearby restaurant when he heard the officers yelling "Drop the knife."
"In a sense they were pleading with him, they don't want to use any force, they don't want to have to shoot him. They want him to stay where he is," he told jurors.
He testified he couldn't seen Carby's right hand from where he was, and he did not see a knife.
Investigators found seven bullet casings and one live bullet, apparently ejected when the first officer attempted to fire and his gun "jammed," jurors heard.
Carby was hit by three of those seven - once in the arm, once in the chest and once in the back. The latter two were fatal, Blain told jurors in his opening summary.

Carby was depressed and suicidal at the time, jurors were told. He had been hospitalized four times before that, under the care of a psychiatrist. He had attempted suicide several times. He tried to cut his neck, he took drugs mixed with bleach and gasoline, he thought about jumping in front of a subway train, and he had tried to disarm a police officer, jurors heard.
